extracted.intended_audience: software developers and hobbyists implementing comic book readers or packaging digital comics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to package digital comic books (.cbz/.cbr etc.) so readers can discover title, issue and page order; and how readers should robustly handle archives and image files. Focuses on using simple in-archive metadata (YAML/JSON) and compatibility considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No standard for comic book archives
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no actual standard for comic book archives; .cbz/.cbr are merely container conventions and can be zip, rar, 7z, tar, or ace — and there is no standardized metadata scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that lack of a standard is the root cause of many interoperability problems; design readers and packaging schemes with this reality in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle multiple archive/container types
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't know what archive type the file will be — different extensions map to different container formats (zip, rar, 7z, tar, ace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on file extension. Use robust libraries that can detect and read common archive formats so readers can open a variety of container types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support multiple and mixed image formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Image formats inside archives can be anything from JPEGs to animated GIFs, and several formats may coexist in the same archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should support a wide range of image formats (including animated formats) and handle archives containing mixed image types without failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on filenames as authoritative metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: There is absolutely no metadata beyond the image file names, so readers have no reliable way of knowing which page is which beyond guessing from file names (which often are page numbers but are not guaranteed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat filenames as a best-effort fallback only. Provide and prefer an explicit metadata mapping for page order and other attributes rather than inferring from filenames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include explicit metadata (series/title/issue) inside the archive
rubrics_metrics.description: Archives typically lack title or issue information, forcing guesses from filenames; include an internal metadata file to convey series, title and issue number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Store a simple metadata file (YAML or JSON) inside the archive with fields such as:
series: "Saga"
title: "Saga #54"
issue: 54
This makes title/issue discoverable without filename heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, portable metadata formats (YAML/JSON)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple YAML or JSON file inside the comic book archive is proposed as the metadata carrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a human-readable, widely-supported format (YAML or JSON) so metadata is easy to generate and parse. Keep the schema minimal to maximize portability and adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design metadata for backward compatibility (ignored by unsupported readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata should be optional and non-breaking; readers that don't support the metadata should simply ignore it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metadata files and their placement do not interfere with existing readers: make them optional and well-named so legacy readers continue to work while newer readers can take advantage of the extra data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit page-order mapping in metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Because filename-based ordering is unreliable, metadata should indicate explicit page ordering to avoid ambiguous or incorrect page sequencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a mapping (e.g., an array of filenames in reading order or page numbers associated with files) in the metadata so readers can render pages in the intended sequence rather than guessing from names.
